strongest_narrative_clusters: everyday goods as a readable currency of life
pollution and carbon translated into human-scale units
how a good index is designed, and how it gets gamed
modern AI benchmarks as the newest index culture
weak_or_repetitive_material: multiple repeated TOC variants covering the same core examples
generic primers on what an index is
owner-project framing that tries to make the book serve 1D3X or POP first
long lists of secondary Russian-language explainers repeating the same weird-index anecdotes
strongest_surprising_hooks: The real price of a phone is not dollars, but hours of life.
Air pollution can become legible when expressed in cigarettes—if the analogy is handled honestly.
A burger and a freight benchmark can tell opposite sides of the same global economy.
Some famous indices are better as myths worth debunking than as tools worth trusting.
Modern AI culture is creating its own index obsession.
evidence_risk_areas: Lipstick, hemline, men’s underwear and hot-waitress style indicators are not strong enough to present as hard economics.
Environmental equivalence claims must preserve analogy boundaries and avoid literal-health overclaiming.
Many cited sources are secondary explainers or media roundups rather than primary methodology pages.
AI benchmark sections can expand scope too far unless kept as a late or optional cluster.
Owner-project examples need explicit neutrality to avoid sounding like content marketing.
high_visual_potential: work-hours comparisons for iPhone or Big Mac
city cards for taxi, haircut and date-night affordability
Big Mac versus Baltic Dry juxtaposition
index trust labels from robust benchmark to folklore
likely_exclusions: owner-project promotion sections centered on POP or SPIKE
deep API/source-catalog appendices that belong in research notes, not the commercial narrative
large generic introductions to index theory unless rewritten sharply
AI ethics and governance material that is disconnected from the main unusual-indices promise
normalization_value_note: The corpus is already structured enough for BookSpec and market-positioning work through metadata filtering and explicit object review; semantic retrieval is not yet justified.
